title: Algorithm-Augmented Work and Domain Experience: The Countervailing Forces of Ability and Aversion
pub: Organization Science, vol. 33, no. 1, pp. 149-169 (2022); DOI 10.1287/orsc.2021.1554 (also Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 20-012)
author: Ryan Allen · Prithwiraj Choudhury

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s claim that algorithm-augmented performance depends on user capability rather than tool access alone, and materially extends it with a framework explaining how domain experience can produce countervailing effects through greater ability and greater aversion. It is not legal-specific and does not address verification or apprenticeship directly, but provides a concrete mechanism for the cluster’s account of uneven user outcomes.
qs: Existing work has focused on the role of domain experience in  achieving human-algorithm complementarities, with mixed perspectives on whether domain experience increases  or inhibits algorithm-augmented performance.
By proposing a unifying framework of how domain experience  affects performance via countervailing mechanisms—ability and aversion—we help reconcile these perspectives.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that algorithmic gains depend on the specific human–AI configuration and materially extends the cluster by showing a non-monotonic experience effect: moderately experienced workers benefited most, while novices lacked evaluative ability and experts sometimes rejected sound advice because of aversion and accountability. Its recommendation for experience-specific transparency and human control adds concrete guidance for selective deployment and interaction design, though the evidence comes from corporate IT support rather than legal work.
qs: We confirm that the difference between performance with the algorithmic tool versus without the tool was characterized by an inverted U-shape over the range of domain experience.
A key  insight is that effective interventions may look quite different for employees with different levels of experience.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports evaluating algorithm-assisted work through direct manual-versus-assisted comparisons while accounting for worker experience and research-design limitations. However, because the supplied excerpts report no performance outcomes, it does not establish whether assistance saved or consumed time or how domain experience changed productivity.
qs: Each participant was assigned tickets to resolve using both the manual ticket resolution system and the  new AutomateIT tool.
Given practical limitations at the company, the intervention was not a  perfectly designed experiment.

kp.k: Experience creates countervailing ability and aversion effects
kp.d: Allen and Choudhury develop a framework in which domain experience improves workers’ ability to assess and complement algorithmic recommendations, but can also increase rejection of accurate advice. They hypothesize that diminishing returns to learning-by-doing, combined with stronger aversion among experts, produce an inverted U-shaped relationship between experience and algorithm-assisted performance relative to manual performance. This is a framework tested in IT support, not direct evidence about legal services.
qs: Reconciling these perspectives, we theorize that intermediate levels of domain experience are optimal for algorithm-augmented performance, due to the interplay between two countervailing forces—ability and aversion.

While domain experience can increase performance via increased ability to complement algorithmic advice (e.g., identifying inaccurate predictions), it can also decrease performance via increased aversion to accurate algorithmic advice.

kp.k: Automation retained consequential human selection and checking
kp.d: At the pseudonymous Indian technology company TECHCO, AutomateIT matched help-ticket text to runbooks and automated execution after human selection. Its model used more than one million labeled help tickets and approximately 7,000 runbook solutions. Workers still selected recommendations and inspected or adjusted execution parameters. Thus, the intervention combined recommendation and execution automation with human oversight rather than replacing the entire task.
qs: The tool automates both of the core steps of the IT ticket resolution process: runbook search and runbook execution.
After a human selects a runbook from the list, the tool is equipped with software that automatically executes the runbook to resolve the ticket.
Before executing the runbook, the user inspects the default parameter values of the automated runbook to see if the parameter inputs will correctly resolve the ticket.

kp.k: Within-subject experiment compared assisted and manual resolution
kp.d: Of 154 volunteers, 153 participated after one hour of tool training. Five sessions over one week each allowed four hours to complete eight assigned tickets, intended as four problems presented in both manual and automated modes with changed parameters. The analysis included 1,224 ticket observations. Domain experience, measured as total years of IT experience, was not randomly assigned. Some assignments departed from the repeated-ticket design; overall, 126 tickets were not repeated.
qs: There were 154 TECHCO IT support staff members who volunteered to participate in the experiment.
Among those who volunteered and received training, all but one participated (he/she called in sick).
Each volunteer was given one hour of training on how to use the new AutomateIT tool prior to the experiment.

Since it was not possible to randomly assign domain experience, we treat domain experience as a moderating effect on performance for tickets resolved using self-judgment (control) vs. algorithm-augmentation (treatment).

kp.k: Average results concealed substantial experience-dependent differences
kp.d: Table 1 reports ticket-resolution rates of 0.703 with AutomateIT and 0.68 manually, a statistically insignificant difference (p=0.387). Table 3’s all-ticket models estimate assisted-versus-manual differences of −0.212 for workers with 0–3 years of experience, +0.162 for 4–6 years, +0.198 for 7–9 years, and −0.051 for 10+ years. The first three estimates were statistically significant; the last was not. These are differences in resolution probability, not measures of time savings or overall occupational productivity.
qs: Only workers with moderate domain experience did significantly better using the algorithm than resolving tickets manually.
High experience workers did about the same with the algorithmic tool, and the lowest experience workers did worse

kp.k: Robustness checks supported the pattern with qualifications
kp.d: The authors tested the relationship using controls, problem or participant fixed effects, experience-group subsamples, first-appearance tickets, Level 2 employees alone, Simonsohn’s two-lines test, and random forests. They report support for the inverted U-shaped pattern, although the quadratic interaction was only marginally significant with problem fixed effects. First-appearance results also differed from the full sample: the 4–6-year group’s estimated effect was −0.006 and insignificant, while the 7–9-year group retained a significant positive effect of 0.211. Ticket assignment differed by employee level, and ticket order was imbalanced; these were addressed analytically rather than eliminated by design.
qs: The random forest algorithm independently found the same inverted U-shaped relationship further validating that we fit a reasonable model to the data
The ticket order of AutomateIT tickets are not evenly distributed across participants with varying levels of domain experience.

kp.k: Rejecting correct recommendations explained much underperformance
kp.d: The tool’s top recommendation was correct approximately 90% of the time, with similar accuracy across experience groups, and proctors ensured that a correct runbook appeared among each ticket’s options. Both low- and high-experience workers frequently released tickets rather than selecting a runbook, leaving those tickets unresolved in the experiment. The authors report that 79% of what they label errors of commission arose from releasing tickets. These between-participant mechanism analyses were exploratory, not experimental identification of ability or aversion.
qs: Participants were not told exactly how accurate the tool would be (about 90% of top recommendations were correct).
these analyses no longer rely on the study’s within-participant randomization, and are best viewed as exploratory analyses rather than experimental evidence
This visual confirms that the rate of the algorithm’s accuracy was similar for all groups, so this was not a driving factor of the results

kp.k: Novices lacked confidence in assessing algorithmic advice
kp.d: Interviews suggested that less experienced workers released tickets because they could not assess recommendations and expected correcting a wrong automated action to be costlier than resolving the problem manually. Their uncertainty was compounded by not knowing the tool’s baseline accuracy. Lower-experience participants released tickets that took peers, on average, nine minutes longer to resolve than attempted tickets; this was an indirect difficulty measure, not observed time spent deciding to release. The authors propose that uncertain algorithm quality and higher error costs increase novice noncompliance.
qs: Because they thought it would be easier to manually resolve the ticket correctly the first time, rather than having to go back to fix it if the algorithm got it wrong, they released tickets they couldn’t evaluate.
This was exacerbated by the fact that they didn’t have a precise idea of the algorithm’s baseline performance compared to their own baseline performance

kp.k: Experts linked resistance to accountability and opaque execution
kp.d: Experienced interviewees described greater knowledge of interconnected systems, trust in their own ability to resolve problems safely, and accountability for unintended consequences. These accounts suggested why experts rejected useful recommendations despite possessing greater complementary ability. Experienced workers did not disproportionately release tickets that peers took longer to solve, and performance on attempted tickets rose with experience, consistent with—but not proving—the proposed mechanism. The study could not distinguish distrust of recommendations from distrust of automated execution.
qs: These highly experienced employees released tickets not because they did not know what was going on, but rather because they trusted their own ability to cleanly resolve the ticket more than the algorithm.
This sense of accountability seemed to be a meaningful driver of algorithm aversion for the most experienced workers.
we do not observe whether high experience workers’ algorithm aversion is because they do not trust the algorithm’s advice or because they do not trust the black-box algorithm to execute it correctly.

kp.k: Resistance arose without perceived job or status threats
kp.d: Participants reported welcoming automation of menial ticket work, which accounted for roughly 25% of their day, and did not report feeling that their jobs were threatened. The authors therefore distinguish their observed aversion from resistance caused by threatened livelihoods, professional status, or investments in existing skills. They separately predict that such threats could strengthen expert aversion in other settings.
qs: In field interviews, participants expressed that they did not feel that their jobs were threatened by the tool, but rather viewed the tool as a welcome automation of menial tasks so they could focus on other aspects of their job.
Yet there was still aversion from more experienced workers

kp.k: Recommended interventions differ by experience level
kp.d: The authors recommend greater transparency and human control for experienced workers, allowing them to interrogate recommendations while retaining responsibility. For novices, they suggest reducing the cost of accepting incorrect advice and training workers on baseline algorithm quality. These are proposed interventions rather than experimentally demonstrated remedies. Encouraging novice compliance is explicitly conditional on the algorithm outperforming those workers.
qs: A key insight is that effective interventions may look quite different for employees with different levels of experience.
One intervention could be to design algorithmic tools and processes with greater transparency, and with greater human control over the algorithmic actions.
First, we suggest lowering the cost of accepting inaccurate algorithmic advice.
These interventions will be applicable in settings where greater algorithmic compliance is actually desirable—i.e., the algorithm tends to outperform workers with low experience.

kp.k: Context and study duration constrain generalization
kp.d: The authors expect the balance of ability and aversion to vary with professional-identity threats, algorithm transparency, human control, perceived accuracy, and the extent to which experience genuinely develops skill. These are predictions about scope conditions, not tested treatment effects. The experiment lasted four hours, used an objectively measurable resolution outcome, and involved workers aged 23–35 without exact age data. It does not establish long-term learning, workforce displacement, or effects on legal work.
qs: Due to such contextual dependencies, our study takes no general stance on whether algorithm-augmented performance will be worse than (or significantly better than) self-performance.
First, our study was bounded in time—a four-hour experimental session.

Future work should explore whether the observed effects persist after several days, weeks, or months, and how quickly workers with varying levels of experience learn to trust (or mistrust) an algorithm.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Allen and Choudhury find that algorithmic assistance benefits moderately experienced IT support workers most, rather than uniformly improving performance or disproportionately benefiting experts.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of corporate IT support, not legal services or generative AI. The authors theorize and report an inverted U-shaped relationship between domain experience and the improvement in ticket resolution with AutomateIT relative to manual work. Experience improves workers’ ability to assess and use recommendations, but greater expert aversion can offset that advantage. In the full-sample experience-group regressions, assistance changes the probability of resolution by approximately −21.2 percentage points for workers with 0–3 years of experience, +16.2 points for 4–6 years, +19.8 points for 7–9 years, and −5.1 points for 10 or more years; the last difference is not statistically significant. The authors interpret exploratory analyses and interviews as suggesting that novices reject advice because they cannot confidently assess it, whereas experts discount advice because of perceived superior contextual understanding and accountability for unintended consequences. They propose experience-specific interventions: transparency and control for experts, and training on baseline algorithmic accuracy and reduced costs of errors for novices. Those interventions are predictions, not tested findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a within-subjects experiment, supplemented by exploratory log analyses and participant interviews; the mechanisms and proposed interventions have a different evidentiary status from the main performance comparison.
pts.d: At TECHCO, a large Indian technology company, 153 participating IT support workers generated 1,224 ticket observations. Each was assigned four manual and four algorithm-assisted tickets, intended to repeat the same four problems with minor parameter changes. AutomateIT matched ticket text to runbooks and executed a human-selected solution after parameter inspection or adjustment. Top recommendations were correct approximately 90% of the time, and proctors ensured that the correct runbook appeared among the options. Overall resolution rates were 70.3% with AutomateIT and 68.0% manually, a statistically insignificant difference (p = 0.387), masking variation by experience. Regression models, experience-group analyses, first-appearance-only checks, a Level 2 employee subsample, a two-lines test, and random forest analyses support the reported pattern. In first-appearance-only results, however, the 4–6-year group’s benefit is not significant; the 7–9-year group’s benefit remains significant. Experience was not randomly assigned. The authors explicitly classify mechanism analyses as exploratory rather than experimental evidence. Interviews support their proposed explanations, but the study does not distinguish distrust of recommendations from distrust of automated execution.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The finding concerns initial use during a four-hour experiment; the authors make contextual, conditional predictions rather than a dated forecast of automation or universal performance gains.
pts.d: Participants received one hour of tool training before a four-hour session, with five sessions conducted over one week. The authors do not establish whether the pattern persists after days, weeks, or months of use. Their setting involved relatively accurate recommendations, human selection and parameter checking, and no precise disclosure of baseline algorithmic accuracy to participants. They predict that threats to professional identity or livelihood could strengthen expert aversion; transparency, control, and accurately perceived higher algorithmic accuracy could flatten the inverted U-shaped relationship. They also suggest that high causal ambiguity can limit learning-by-doing and allow aversion to outweigh ability sooner. Recommendations encouraging novice compliance are explicitly conditional on the algorithm outperforming those workers. No specific empirical fieldwork date or long-term adoption timetable is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are corporate IT support workers at different experience levels and managers designing human–algorithm workflows, not legal practitioners or legal-service buyers.
pts.d: The sample spans 0–15 years of IT experience across three employee levels at a company with more than 100,000 employees and approximately 500 IT support staff. Novices can lose performance when they cannot assess recommendations; moderately experienced workers gain resolution performance; experts possess complementary ability but may forgo gains through rejection of correct advice. Managers are advised to tailor implementation to these distinct constraints rather than treating all workers alike. Human involvement remains essential in this workflow: workers select a runbook and inspect or modify parameters before execution. Participants reportedly regarded the tool as relief from menial work rather than a threat to their jobs; ticket resolution occupied about 25% of their day. The paper does not establish job displacement, staffing reductions, legal-market effects, or effects on access to justice.
